comparator.name: Health and Society
comparator.sourceNotes: Current BGM 2026 handbook:132 compulsory taught credits +18 compulsory thesis +30 open choice=180; no formal track selected. Two additional zero-credit safety obligations. Complete all132 taught credits, including all60 first-year credits, before the thesis in this coherent example; this exceeds the current102-prescribed-credit threshold and includes YRM21806 Data Analysis and HSO31306 Literature Reviews. YSS84818 requires the named Health and Society thesis guide; its publicly indexed same-code guide has2023 logistical dates, not asserted a new2026 publication. Its102/allB1/data-analysis entry rules are satisfied by the completed prescribed course set; current2026 programme/module rules control. No specific chair-topic or obsolete dated timetable is imposed. Current module content and programme sequencing resolve the pathway without an invented new source gate.
components: The programme approaches health through society, behaviour, prevention and health systems. General safety is an additional zero-credit requirement.
Research Methods in the Social Sciences
Global Challenges and Communication in a Changing World
Introduction to Epidemiology and Public Health
Includes field research on environmental determinants and healthy neighbourhood design. Complete the additional zero-credit fieldwork safety requirement before field activities.
Preventing Disease and Improving Population Health: an Interdisciplinary Approach
Health Demography and Global Population Transitions
Population-health research uses quantitative methods alongside the concurrently taught Data Analysis course.
Data Analysis for Health and Society
Literature Reviews for Health and Society
Required third-year preparation in systematic and scoping literature reviews and critical appraisal.

Required 18-credit independent research project, combining a literature review with empirical research, a report and oral presentation and defence. Complete at least 102 prescribed credits, including all first-year credits, before starting. This example completes the prescribed taught courses first, including Data Analysis and Literature Reviews.
Thirty credits of minor and/or elective study complete the bachelor. The choice remains open; examples of possible minors are not compulsory routes.

alternatives.label: Population health, behaviour and social policy
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum sustains the named health/social-science, policy or behavioural-communication priorities; it is not a biomedical or clinical qualification.
alternatives.concept: Investigate population health through epidemiology, health and social psychology, social inequality, public economics and policy. Combine quantitative, qualitative and review methods with environmental governance and persuasion to examine prevention and healthier communities.
progression: Current workbook offerings, earlier formal prerequisites, Year-1 PPD, 24 courses/four per term/180 EC and at least six advanced courses verified; foundational research and subject courses precede related advanced work where feasible.

alternatives.label: Health inequalities, institutions and public policy
alternatives.concept: Investigate how inequality, institutions and collective decisions shape health and access to resources. Combine public health and health psychology with sociology, law, public economics, EU and policy analysis, environmental justice, organisational evidence and quantitative and qualitative research.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum sustains the named health/social-science, policy or behavioural-communication priorities; it is not a biomedical or clinical qualification.
alternatives.distinctness: This programme gives 45 EC of different study to law, environmental justice, EU institutions, econometrics, inclusive leadership and racial representation. It makes inequality and public institutions the sustained priority, with six courses different from the closest programme and twelve from the communication programme.
progression: Current workbook offerings, earlier formal prerequisites, Year-1 PPD, 24 courses/four per term/180 EC and at least six advanced courses verified; foundational research and subject courses precede related advanced work where feasible.

alternatives.label: Health behaviour, evidence and public communication
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum sustains the named health/social-science, policy or behavioural-communication priorities; it is not a biomedical or clinical qualification.
alternatives.concept: Investigate health behaviour through social, health and developmental psychology, epidemiology and evidence synthesis. Combine persuasion, misinformation analysis and community communication with practical audience-adapted work and youth-prevention research; climate and media projects supply complementary settings for these communication methods.
progression: Current workbook offerings, earlier formal prerequisites, Year-1 PPD, 24 courses/four per term/180 EC and at least six advanced courses verified; foundational research and subject courses precede related advanced work where feasible.
alternatives.distinctness: This programme prioritises behavioural evidence and public communication through developmental psychology, research synthesis, persuasion, misinformation, youth-prevention tools and audience-adapted community/media work. Seven courses differ from the closest programme and twelve from the policy programme; the changes implement the behavioural-communication priority.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Population health, epidemiology, prevention and global health
Health sociology, inequalities, social determinants and community health
Health psychology, lifestyle choices, food behaviour and behaviour change
Health economics, policy, management and healthcare organisations
Statistics, qualitative and quantitative methods, intervention evaluation and independent research
adjacent: Health inequalities, wellbeing and social policy
questions: How do social, behavioural and environmental factors shape population health?
How can evidence-based interventions support healthier choices and communities?
How can policy and organisations reduce health inequalities?

selection.assessment: The closest response sustains population health, social/behavioural determinants, policy and evidence. The inequality/institutions programme then prioritises legal, redistributive and collective governance questions; the behaviour/communication programme changes the priority to behavioural evidence and audience-directed interventions. Pairwise differences are6/7/12courses (45/52.5/90EC), with9/9/7advanced courses and current feasible schedules. All twelve generator interests have exact ownership. The alternative healthy-environment theme is already addressed by the closest and policy programmes; no unrelated fourth programme is manufactured.

trace: Scarcity, incentives, consumer choice and market behaviour provide an economic foundation for resource-allocation and policy questions; no health-economic evaluation technique is inferred.

Public goods, externalities, efficiency/equity, health and welfare expenditure, insurance and redistribution directly support health-policy allocation questions; not a dedicated cost-effectiveness course.
OLS, GLS, instrumental variables, inference, causal/predictive economic modelling and an empirical paper support evaluating social-policy evidence; given full weight from the official description.
Research questions, measurement, surveys, experiments, inferential statistics and an ethical empirical project directly supply social/behavioural research foundations.
Belonging, identity safety, inclusion, emotional regulation and an original survey project support wellbeing and unequal social environments and develop empirical behavioural evidence.

Organisational structure, culture, teams, change and workplace health, with systematic-review practice, support understanding health organisations; patient-centred healthcare innovation remains a different specialism.
R cleaning, manipulation, visualisation and spatial/text data analysis support empirical health and social research; this complements rather than replaces inferential statistics.

Institutions, actors, participation, public goods and policy advice/evaluation on food, water, energy and climate support collective decisions about healthy environments; no direct urban-health fieldwork equivalence.
Climate impacts including health, climate justice, adaptation and stakeholder communication provide a substantive environmental-health context; not a neighbourhood health-design course.
Medical and climate misinformation, scientific credibility, diffusion and research-grounded debunking messages directly support critical public-health communication and trust.
Rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender in law supply legal/normative tools for analysing unequal institutions; no specific health regulation is claimed.
Moral argument, care ethics, autonomy and justice-related reasoning provide substantive ethical tools for contested health decisions, without claiming a specialist health-law curriculum.
Political institutions, representation, interests and empirical comparative analysis provide the political framework in which collective health-policy choices occur.
EU institutions, interests, legislation and implementation supply a specific supranational level of health-relevant governance; health policy is an application, not the entire course.

The official description supports policy-making phases across national/international arenas, a sugar case and policy-memo writing. These directly support policy analysis; no unlisted health-policy theory or method is inferred.

Social structure, stratification, class, race, gender and inequality provide substantive sociological tools for analysing social determinants of health; applications are broader than health sociology.
Interviews, focus groups, ethics, reflexivity, coding and a qualitative research project directly support inquiry into lived health, community practices and unequal environments.
Intersectionality, stigma, othering, social space, gender and colonial power deepen the theoretical analysis of structural health inequality; not a specialist public-health course.

Description-supported movement theory and environmental justice, including feminist and anti-colonial perspectives, directly deepen collective-action and unequal-environment analysis; absent outline detail is not invented.
Civil society, trust, solidarity, public spheres and empirical study of civic organisations supply specific methods and theory for community participation and collective health action.
Direct epidemiology, disease measures, bias and causality, social/environmental determinants and a local population-health intervention project supply the public-health core.
Psychological and neural explanations of learning, social influence and mental processes provide the gateway to health and behavioural psychology; not an introduction to population-health systems.
Social influence, attitudes, persuasion, prejudice and group behaviour directly support understanding health choices and social intervention; the research-design task develops evidence appraisal.

Research design, regression, group comparisons, logistic models, reliability and R analysis support evaluating health and behavioural evidence; no claim of full epidemiological or qualitative-methods coverage.
Biopsychosocial health, inequalities, health behaviours, prevention, stress, coping and patient communication directly implement health psychology; clinical settings are one part of its content.
Systematic review, study selection, risk of bias, effect sizes and R meta-analysis directly support critical synthesis of health/behavioural intervention evidence.

Development across the lifespan, environmental influences, care and a life-story interview support age-sensitive understanding of health and behaviour. Individual development is not health demography.

Research-based youth prevention, mental wellbeing, school inclusion, media literacy and feedback-revised educational tools support evidence-informed community intervention. Radicalisation is a specific application, not the health programme’s defining topic.
Rhetorical argument, persuasion, speeches and audience-directed educational storytelling provide communication practice supporting public explanation and behaviour-change messages.

Description-supported analysis of contested climate communication across texts, films and social media, culminating in participation in public debate, complements public-health/environmental communication questions.

Community work with children designs and revises age-appropriate rhetorical teaching activities. This specifically complements audience-sensitive intervention communication, not clinical or health-intervention expertise.

Ethical persuasion, framing, cognitive shortcuts and applied community messaging on sustainable lifestyles provide a specific behaviour-change communication contribution. Health intervention mapping is not reproduced.

Disability representation, media stereotypes, authentic voice and inclusive futures provide substantive critical analysis of how mediated messages shape attitudes toward wellbeing and marginalised groups.

Systemic racial construction, exclusion, marginalized voices and participatory/archival media inquiry supply a sustained social-inequality and representation contribution; not a claim of health-specific communication training.

Documentary research, interviewing, representation ethics and producing a short film supply complementary practical tools for communicating social/health evidence; no compulsory health film is assumed.
blocks: Both teach disease measures, epidemiological study designs, bias and public-health evidence. The programmes differ in applications and scope.
Both directly teach social influence, attitudes, group behaviour and the social-psychological study of behaviour.
Both directly study health behaviour, stress and coping, mental health and biopsychosocial evidence. UCR also emphasises patients and medical settings; WUR includes a quantitative group study.

The UCR programme combines public health and social sciences across several courses. No single selected course integrates the WUR introduction’s health systems, history, prevention and societal determinants.
No selected course provides the full global-health and health-promotion framework, international priority setting and health-system collaboration.
Social and health psychology contribute to behaviour, but no selected course sustains the specific biological, psychological and socioeconomic study of nutrition behaviour.
Climate and governance courses support environmental-health interests but do not reproduce the integrated neighbourhood health field-research and healthy-design assignment.
Public health, health psychology and communication contribute to prevention, but no single separately placed course integrates the WUR multilevel infectious/chronic disease-prevention framework.
Lifespan psychology studies individual development; it does not supply population demographic measures, transitions and quantitative health-demography research.

Public goods, equity, redistribution, health expenditure and social insurance directly address public allocation for a healthy society. WUR additionally teaches dedicated health-economic evaluation and wider economic perspectives.
Organisational culture, collaboration, leadership and change address an important organisational part of healthcare innovation. WUR’s patient-centred and frugal innovation design is not reproduced.

Misinformation, scientific trust, cognitive/social vulnerabilities and health/climate communication address an important part of the WUR course. WUR additionally teaches agenda setting, media and political communication across countries.

Ethical theory and critical moral argument supply a central part of reasoning about health, justice and autonomy. WUR concentrates on health-policy dilemmas; UCR has broader philosophical applications.

Policy-making phases, national/international arenas, a sugar-policy case and policy memos directly address policy analysis. WUR focuses more fully on health systems, participatory health promotion and policy networks.
Both teach sociological theory, social structure and inequality. WUR applies these throughout to health; UCR develops broader social cases.
Speech preparation and delivery, persuasive appeals and feedback-based communication practice address the specific presentation-skills function. UCR is a larger rhetoric course.

Theory-based persuasive messages, implementation with community partners and reflective evaluation address the communication part of behaviour-change intervention. WUR additionally requires systematic health Intervention Mapping and broader determinant/implementation planning.
No selected course provides the dedicated historical study of demographic, epidemiological, nutritional and welfare-state transitions.
No selected course sustains the specific sociological study of eating customs, food identity, access and health across cultural settings.
Both develop research questions and social-science research design, including experimental and nonexperimental approaches. The UCR course adds statistical analysis and an empirical project.

Regression, group comparisons, categorical outcomes and R-based research analysis share substantial quantitative methods. WUR also integrates qualitative analysis, mixed methods and survival analysis.
Both teach systematic literature searching, selection and critical evidence appraisal. UCR additionally develops quantitative meta-analysis; WUR also teaches scoping reviews.

Foundational statistical content occurs within broader selected methods courses, which are placed against their strongest research-design and data-analysis relationships; no separate course is duplicated here.
Inference and regression occur in the selected methods sequence. Those courses are placed against research design and data analysis rather than duplicated as a separate statistics course.
The required 18-credit WUR thesis differs from scheduled UCR courses. Optional UCR independent research is shown separately, outside each 180-credit programme.
This is genuine open elective space, without an invented course counterpart.

notes.text: Wageningen offers a dedicated social-scientific health curriculum with nutrition behaviour, population demography, healthy-environment fieldwork, health intervention design and a required 18-credit thesis. UCR develops substantial public health, psychology, sociology, policy and communication, but does not reproduce that full specialist sequence. Optional UCR independent research is additional to each 180-credit schedule.

audience.programmeDescription: Health and Society studies how behaviour, social conditions, environments and public decisions shape health. Psychology, sociology, economics and research methods support prevention, healthier communities and health policy.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The three UCR programmes approach these interests through population health and social policy, inequality and public institutions, or behavioural evidence and public communication. Dedicated nutrition, health demography, healthy-neighbourhood fieldwork, systematic health-intervention design and the required thesis remain important differences.

curriculum.limitation: The bachelor comprises 132 credits of prescribed taught courses, an 18-credit thesis and 30 credits of minor and/or electives. Safety requirements carry no additional credits. The thesis follows the required preparation and completed first-year study.
